methodological_rigor.justification: This is a well-designed retrospective registry-based cohort study with a large real-world dataset (116,217 co-test samples) and long passive follow-up through December 2025. The four-category co-test classification is clinically logical, eligibility criteria are clearly defined, and outcome ascertainment uses deterministic linkage via a regional pathology information system. Key limitations are acknowledged: unit of analysis is the co-test sample rather than the individual (allowing multiple contributions per woman), verification bias is present as test-positive women are more likely to undergo biopsy, and HPV DNA co-testing data were unavailable for most of the cohort. The retrospective single-center design limits generalizability.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The study directly addresses a clinically important question in cervical cancer prevention: whether genotype-specific HPV mRNA co-testing with cytology improves risk stratification in routine practice. The findings are immediately translatable, providing absolute risk estimates for CIN2+, CIN3+, and cervical cancer across four co-test categories that can inform clinical follow-up protocols. The identification of a small but high-risk NILM/mRNA+ subgroup (1.3% of NILM, capturing 42.7% of CIN3+ within NILM) is clinically actionable. The study is relevant to settings still using cytology-based screening or transitional HPV DNA programs globally.

reporting_quality.justification: The manuscript adheres well to STROBE criteria for observational cohort studies: clear study design description, detailed eligibility criteria, explicit outcome definitions, data sources, statistical methods with confidence intervals and effect sizes including risk ratios and absolute risk differences. Ethics approval and data protection are documented. Minor gaps include the absence of a CONSORT/STROBE checklist and limited information on temporal changes in screening policy during the follow-up period. Data are not publicly deposited; the study uses a local laboratory information system (SymPathy) and patient-level data are de-identified but not shared, resulting in a low data availability score.

novelty_literature.justification: The study extends existing evidence on HPV mRNA co-testing in a Norwegian regional cohort with unusually large sample size and long follow-up. The genotype-specific risk hierarchy (HPV16 > HPV18 > HPV45) and the disproportionate capture of CIN3+ within NILM are clinically informative but broadly consistent with prior Norwegian mRNA studies. The novelty lies primarily in scale and real-world representativeness rather than a conceptually new finding. The use of mutually exclusive genotype-combination groups in Table 6 adds an incremental analytical contribution. The study does not introduce a new test or mechanism, and similar risk stratification principles have been previously demonstrated.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written with well-organized sections and clinically interpretable risk data presented in a logical sequence. The abstract accurately reflects the findings. Tables are described sufficiently in the text. The authors appropriately distinguish their co-testing strategy from universal HPV DNA co-testing throughout the manuscript. Limitations are discussed honestly and in appropriate detail. Minor weaknesses include some repetition between the abstract and main text, and the discussion occasionally recites prior literature without adding new synthesis.

key_strengths: Very large real-world cohort (116,217 co-test samples) with long passive follow-up through December 2025 from a population-based screening registry
Clinically interpretable absolute risk estimates across four clearly defined co-test categories, directly applicable to screening and follow-up decisions
Identification of a high-risk NILM/mRNA+ subgroup capturing 42.7% of CIN3+ within NILM cytology despite representing only 1.3% of NILM samples
Genotype-specific analyses with mutually exclusive combination groups add biological plausibility and clinical granularity beyond binary test positivity
Thorough limitation discussion including verification bias, unit-of-analysis issue, and absence of HPV DNA comparator data
key_concerns: Unit of analysis is the co-test sample rather than the individual woman, inflating event counts and precluding individual-level risk estimates
Verification bias: women with positive test results are substantially more likely to undergo biopsy, likely inflating risk estimates in test-positive groups
HPV DNA test results unavailable for most of the cohort, preventing direct comparison with the current standard of care (primary HPV DNA screening)
Single-center, single-region design from Northern Norway limits generalizability to other settings and ethnicities
Analyses are descriptive and cross-tabulation-based; no survival analysis or time-to-event modeling was performed to account for differential follow-up duration
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a competent, well-executed real-world cohort study with a large dataset and strong clinical relevance for cervical cancer risk stratification. The core findings are incremental extensions of prior Norwegian mRNA work rather than paradigm-shifting, and methodological limitations (verification bias, sample-level analysis) prevent a higher tier assignment. Tier 3 with minor revisions is appropriate.
